client: I've been really stressed out lately because I missed the deadline for my final project at university, and I just can't stop thinking about how badly it's going to tank my grade. Every time I try to sit down and do something about it, I just freeze up and my mind goes blank. Honestly, I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, but I figured I'd give this a shot.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a lot of weight right now — the stress of the missed deadline, the mental freeze when you try to act, and even some doubt about whether this will help. That kind of spiral, where worry makes it harder to move and staying stuck feeds more worry, is really exhausting, and it makes complete sense that you're feeling overwhelmed. I'm glad you gave this a shot anyway — can you tell me a little more about what happens in your body or mind in those moments right before you freeze up?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: Yeah, it's like... right when I open my laptop and pull up the project folder, my chest gets really tight and my thoughts just start racing. I start thinking things like "it's already too late, what's even the point," and then I feel this kind of numbness wash over me and I just close the laptop again. It's like my brain decides the safest option is to just not deal with it at all.
therapist: What you're describing — that tight chest, the racing thoughts, and then the shutdown — is actually your nervous system trying to protect you from something that feels threatening, even if it's making things harder in the long run. That thought "it's already too late, what's even the point" is doing a lot of heavy lifting there, and it's worth gently questioning whether that's actually true or whether it's anxiety talking. What do you think would happen if you pushed back on that thought just a little — is it *really* too late, or does it just feel that way right now?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I mean, logically I know it's probably not completely too late, like the professor hasn't explicitly said there's no way to submit it late. But when I'm actually in that moment, the logical part of my brain just kind of... disappears, and the "what's the point" feeling takes over completely. I guess I'm just not sure how pushing back on the thought is supposed to work when the feeling is so overwhelming that I can't even think straight.
therapist: You're making a really important point — knowing something logically and *feeling* it are two very different things, and it's hard to think your way out of a feeling when the feeling is running the show. I also notice that even as you're describing all this, there's something in how you're speaking that feels almost quiet, maybe a little defeated — like part of you has already braced for the worst. Is that sense of defeat something that's been sitting with you for a while, even underneath the stress?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: Yeah, honestly that hits closer to home than I expected. It's not just about this project — I think I've been walking around with this low-level feeling of "I'm probably going to mess things up" for a while now, and the missed deadline just kind of confirmed it for me. It's like I've been waiting for proof that I can't handle things, and now I have it.
therapist: What you just shared feels really significant — that sense of "I've been waiting to be proven right about myself" is such a painful place to live, and it sounds like it's been there quietly long before this deadline. I'm curious though, because even as you're naming something that feels heavy and confirming, your voice carries an energy that sounds almost urgent, like this realization is stirring something up for you. Does putting words to this pattern for the first time feel like relief, or does it bring up something else?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: It's kind of both, actually — there's a small part of me that feels like "oh, so this is a thing, it has a shape," which is almost a relief. But mostly it just makes me feel kind of exposed and a little scared, like now that I've said it out loud I can't pretend it isn't there anymore. And honestly, part of me is wondering if just naming it is actually going to help, or if I'm going to leave here and still freeze up the next time I open that laptop.
therapist: That feeling of being exposed is actually a really meaningful sign — it means something true got through, and that takes courage, even if it doesn't feel that way right now. You're right that naming it alone won't stop the freeze, but what it does do is give us something to work with, a way to catch that "I'm going to mess things up" story *before* it pulls you under. So rather than leaving today with just insight, what if we spent a little time mapping out one small, concrete step you could take with the project — something tiny enough that the "what's the point" voice doesn't have much to grab onto?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and I'm willing to try, but I guess my worry is that even a "tiny step" is going to feel huge once I'm actually sitting there alone with it. Like, what counts as small enough — because in my head, even just opening the document feels like I'm committing to something I might fail at again. I don't want to set up another situation where I freeze and then feel even worse about myself than I already do.
therapist: The fear you're describing — that even a small step could become another piece of evidence against yourself — makes so much sense given that pattern we just uncovered, and it's actually really wise of you to name that risk rather than just white-knuckling through it. So what if the first step wasn't opening the document at all, but something even further back — like just writing down one sentence about what the project is supposed to be, with the laptop closed? The goal isn't to produce anything, it's just to prove to that "I'll fail" voice that you can touch the thing without it swallowing you whole.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: Okay, that actually sounds a little less terrifying than I expected, and I think I could maybe do that. But I'm already noticing this voice in my head saying "that's so small it doesn't even count, you're just avoiding the real thing," like even trying to make it manageable feels like cheating somehow. Is that normal, or is that just me finding another way to talk myself out of doing anything at all?
therapist: That voice is incredibly common — it's actually a hallmark of the same pattern we've been talking about, where your mind raises the bar just fast enough that nothing you do ever quite counts. The fact that you caught it happening in real time is genuinely significant, because that's exactly the skill that starts to loosen its grip over time. I'm also noticing something in how you're asking that question — there's a softness there, almost like you're hoping to be told it's okay to be kind to yourself — so let me say clearly: it is, and small steps that you actually take will always count more than perfect plans that stay frozen.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: That actually landed in a way I wasn't expecting, and I felt something kind of loosen in my chest when you said it. I think I've been so used to that voice setting impossible standards that I forgot I was even allowed to decide what counts as progress for myself. I'm still a little scared I'll get home and the old feeling will just take over again, but I think I want to try the one-sentence thing tonight and see what happens.
therapist: That loosening in your chest is worth paying attention to — your body is registering something real, even if the scared part is still there alongside it. It makes complete sense that both things are true at once: a genuine shift *and* a worry that the old patterns will be waiting at home, and holding both of those honestly is actually more solid ground than false confidence would be. Before you go, would it help to think of one small thing you could do if the freeze does start to creep in tonight — not to fight it, but just to remind yourself that you get to decide what counts?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: Yeah, I think that could help, though I'm not totally sure what that would look like in practice. Maybe if I feel the freeze coming on, I could just... remind myself that I already did something today by coming here and saying all this out loud, like that counts too. I guess I'm just hoping that in the moment, I'll actually be able to access that thought instead of it getting drowned out by everything else.
therapist: What you just said — that coming here and speaking honestly today already counts — is exactly right, and I want you to hold onto that because it's true. One thing that can help in those frozen moments is to make that reminder as concrete as possible beforehand, almost like leaving yourself a note that says "I already did something hard today, and small counts" somewhere you'll actually see it when you open the laptop. You've done something genuinely meaningful today, and that doesn't disappear just because the night gets harder.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I like the idea of a physical note, actually — it feels less easy to dismiss than just trying to remember something in my head when I'm already spiraling. I think I'll write it on a sticky note and put it on my laptop before I go to bed tonight. I'm still nervous, but I think that's the most okay I've felt about this whole situation in a while.
therapist: The sticky note idea is a really grounded, practical way to make that kindness harder to argue with when your brain is in a tough spot — I love that you landed on that yourself. It sounds like something has genuinely shifted today, even if the nervousness is still there riding alongside the okayness, and both of those can be true at once. Be gentle with yourself tonight, and remember that however the one-sentence exercise goes, you've already shown yourself something important today about your own courage.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech
